featuredIntervention.speaker: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar
featuredIntervention.shortExcerpt: Our difficulty is with regard to the beginning.

speakers.name: Dr. Rajendra Prasad
speakers.positionSummary: Opens the sitting, welcomes Vijayalakshmi Pandit, manages a list of more than fifty prospective speakers and regulates the debate.

speakers.name: M. R. Masani
speakers.positionSummary: Reads the Resolution as a democratic-socialist programme that must combine social transformation with individual liberty and political democracy.

speakers.name: Frank Anthony
speakers.positionSummary: Accepts the republican objective but supports deferring parts of the declaration in the interests of wider agreement.

speakers.name: Syama Prasad Mookerjee
speakers.positionSummary: Argues that the Assembly should proceed despite the Muslim League's absence and ground its authority in the people of India.

speakers.name: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar
speakers.positionSummary: Questions the Resolution's lack of remedies for rights, affirms the possibility of ultimate unity, and argues that the beginning must be inclusive enough to bring reluctant groups in.

speakers.name: Sardar Ujjal Singh
speakers.positionSummary: Supports proceeding with the Resolution while insisting that Sikh and other minority safeguards must be meaningful and satisfactory.

speakers.name: Seth Govind Das
speakers.positionSummary: Speaks in Hindustani, stresses freedom, socialism and democratic aspiration, and rejects external obstruction of the Assembly's work.

interventions.summary: The Chairman welcomes Vijayalakshmi Pandit, resumes the Objectives Resolution debate and explains that more than fifty members have sought to speak, making a practical time limit necessary.

Masani begins from the problem of minorities and nation-building, arguing that constitutional safeguards matter but cannot substitute for the longer social process of becoming one political community.
He interprets the Resolution as democratic socialism: social and economic change pursued through political democracy, dispersed power and protection of the individual against an all-powerful state.

Frank Anthony supports Dr. M. R. Jayakar's amendment. He accepts the republican objective but argues that declaring detailed institutional arrangements should wait for wider participation and agreement.

Mookerjee rejects postponement, arguing that waiting for every absent party would paralyse the Assembly and that the Resolution is not inconsistent with the Assembly's task of framing a free constitution.
He argues that the Assembly must ultimately rely on popular legitimacy, proceed with constitution-making and demonstrate that minorities will be treated justly even if the Muslim League stays away.
interventions.excerpt: Our sanction is the people of India

interventions.summary: Called earlier than expected, Ambedkar says he is speaking without preparation. He separates the Resolution into broadly non-controversial goals and politically controversial opening clauses.
Ambedkar argues that declaring rights is insufficient without remedies. He also questions how social and economic justice can become real without stronger economic commitments.
He says current political, social and economic divisions do not make eventual national unity impossible. The strategic problem is how the common journey begins.
interventions.excerpt: our difficulty is with regard to the beginning

interventions.summary: Ambedkar supports another attempt at accommodation with the Muslim League. He distinguishes possessing power from exercising it wisely and warns against resolving the political conflict through force.

Ujjal Singh supports the Resolution and opposes indefinite postponement. He reads it as a declaration of freedom, Union and social justice while recognising the political difficulty around autonomous units and residuary powers.
He places the Sikh case before the House, recalls earlier assurances and argues that safeguards must secure a meaningful Sikh position within India rather than outside it.
Govind Das chooses to speak in the language of the country and links political freedom with a democratic and socialist social order.
He argues that neither British policy nor Muslim League obstruction should stop the Assembly from pursuing its constitutional work and urges members to treat the Resolution as a serious pledge.
At 1 PM the Chairman adjourns the Assembly until the following morning, noting that the Rules Committee will meet in the afternoon.
